Several OCR characters appear to be misreadings and have been translated by their evident sense: 絨膝 read as 緘縢 "seals and cords", 合 as 令 "magistrate", 晷 as 略 "briefly", 從人 as 從入 "followed him in". The character 雙 in the first line is doubtful, and that clause is rendered tentatively. The title on the book at the end of the page breaks off mid-word and continues on the next page.</meta>

<margin>A cultivated man
wins a cultivated
wife and a cultivated
friend; and a
cultivated girl is written
with a cultivated
brush: a cultivated person,
cultivated speech, cultivated deeds,
cultivated prose. Whoever has
not yet read it has, in all his life,
never seen such a book. This</margin>

...so how could they have stolen them for their own use? He had once stored a separate chest of cups and bowls; its seals and cords were intact as before, yet the vessels had all vanished. As for those who called it wild and unfathomable talk, Liu only laughed, and did not question the matter any further, item by item.

Jiaona <note>original: "嬌娜", the name of the tale's heroine, meaning roughly "Delicate and Graceful"</note>

Scholar Kong Xueli was a descendant of the Sage <note>Confucius, whose family name was Kong</note>. He was a man of refined and gentle bearing, and skilled at poetry. A close friend of his, the magistrate of Tiantai <note>a county in Zhejiang</note>, sent a letter inviting him to come. The scholar went, but the magistrate had just died. Stranded and penniless, unable to return home, he lodged at Putuo Temple, where the monks hired him to copy texts for them. A hundred-odd paces west of the temple stood the mansion of Mr. Shan. Mr. Shan was the son of a high-ranking family; a great lawsuit had brought him to ruin, and with few left in his household he had moved to live in the countryside, so the house stood empty. One day, as heavy snow whirled down and all was silent with not a traveller on the road, Kong happened to pass its gate. A young man came out, of very handsome and elegant appearance. Seeing the scholar, he hurried over to greet him with a bow, offered a few words of sympathy for his plight, and begged him to come inside. The scholar took a liking to him and gladly followed him in. The rooms were not very large, but brocade curtains hung everywhere, and on the walls were many works of calligraphy and painting by old masters. On the desk lay a volume whose label read <term>Langhuan Suo</term> <gloss>"Trifling Records of Langhuan", a fabled library of rare books; the title continues on the next page</gloss>

<summary>This page closes a preceding tale about vessels mysteriously vanishing from a sealed chest, then opens the story "Jiaona". The scholar Kong Xueli, a descendant of Confucius stranded far from home, is invited by a handsome young stranger into an empty mansion near Putuo Temple. A critic's marginal note praises the tale for its refined characters and style.</summary>
<keywords>Pu Songling, Liaozhai Zhiyi, Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio, Jiaona, Kong Xueli, descendant of Confucius, Putuo Temple, Tiantai, Mr. Shan, Langhuan, marginal commentary, refinement, Qing fiction</keywords>
